title: Kubernetes Core Architecture, Control Plane & RBAC
summary: Master core Kubernetes architecture, declarative control plane reconciliation, Deployments, ReplicaSets, ServiceAccounts, least-privilege RBAC Roles, and authorization auditing.
learningObjectives: Deploy, scale, and manage high-availability multi-replica Deployments with rolling update strategies.
Configure least-privilege Role-Based Access Control using ServiceAccounts, Roles, and RoleBindings.
Audit and verify API authorization permissions across namespaces using kubectl auth can-i.

curriculumModules.title: Control Plane Architecture: apiserver, etcd, scheduler & controller-manager
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: The Kubernetes control plane maintains the global cluster state machine. kube-apiserver is the stateless front-end communicating with etcd. kube-scheduler assigns unassigned Pods to healthy nodes based on affinity and resources, while kube-controller-manager runs core reconciliation loops.
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Always deploy a minimum of 3 control plane nodes across distinct availability zones with stacked or external etcd topologies to survive single-node quorum failures.

curriculumModules.title: Workload Controllers: Deployments, ReplicaSets & Rolling Updates
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: Deployments provide declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. By configuring maxSurge and maxUnavailable, platform engineers achieve seamless zero-downtime rolling updates with instant rollback capabilities to prior deployment revisions.
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Configure readiness probes, PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs), and topologySpreadConstraints across availability zones to guarantee continuous availability during voluntary and involuntary disruptions.

curriculumModules.title: RBAC Security: ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings & Authorization Auditing
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) enforces least-privilege access by binding subjects (Users, Groups, ServiceAccounts) to specific API groups, resources, and verbs within a namespace (Role) or across the cluster (ClusterRole).
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Disable default automountServiceAccountToken on workloads and bind dedicated ServiceAccounts with tightly scoped Roles rather than using cluster-admin.

labs.title: Deploying High-Availability Microservices with Zero-Downtime Rollouts
labs.scenario: Deploy the payments-api microservice in namespace core-production with 3 replicas for multi-zone fault tolerance, expose it via a ClusterIP Service on port 8080, and verify rolling update status.
labs.productionContext: High-availability services in production require multiple replicas spread across nodes, coupled with health probes and backing Services to maintain zero dropped requests.

labs.title: Least-Privilege RBAC: ServiceAccount, Role, RoleBinding & Authorization Audit
labs.scenario: Security compliance mandates restricting automated CI/CD access. Provision a dedicated ServiceAccount deploy-bot in namespace staging, grant it scoped permissions to read pods and deployments via Role pod-reader, bind them using RoleBinding deploy-bot-binding, and audit permissions using kubectl auth can-i.
labs.productionContext: Least-privilege RBAC minimizes blast radius in multi-tenant clusters, preventing compromised automation credentials from performing unauthorized mutations or cluster-wide escalations.
objectives: Create namespace staging for isolated environment
Provision ServiceAccount deploy-bot in namespace staging
Create Role pod-reader granting get, list, and watch on pods and deployments
Bind deploy-bot to pod-reader using RoleBinding deploy-bot-binding
Audit permissions using kubectl auth can-i

assessmentQuestions.question: Which Kubernetes control-plane component is exclusively responsible for interacting directly with etcd storage?
assessmentQuestions.explanation: kube-apiserver is the only component in a Kubernetes cluster that communicates directly with the etcd key-value datastore. All other components (scheduler, controller manager, kubelet) communicate with etcd indirectly through the apiserver's REST API.

assessmentQuestions.question: When configuring RBAC in Kubernetes, what is the key difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
options: (Recommended) A Role is scoped to a specific namespace, whereas a ClusterRole applies cluster-wide across all namespaces and cluster-scoped resources like Nodes.
A Role applies to human users, while a ClusterRole applies only to ServiceAccounts.
A Role can only grant read permissions, while a ClusterRole grants write permissions.
A Role is managed by Docker, whereas a ClusterRole is managed by containerd.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Roles are namespace-scoped and grant access only to resources within that single namespace. ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped and can grant access to cluster-wide resources (Nodes, PVs, Namespaces) or serve as reusable permission templates across multiple namespaces when bound via RoleBindings.
